findings.message: The identification header gives the version 16, whose upper four bits name an encapsulation this decoder does not know; RFC 7845 version 1 decoders refuse it (section 5.1).
The identification header gives the version 2, where RFC 7845 writes 1; decoders read it as compatible (section 5.1).
The identification header gives 0 output channels, which RFC 7845 forbids (section 5.1); decoders refuse the stream.
Channel mapping family 0 allows one or two channels, but the header gives 3 (RFC 7845, section 5.1.1.1); decoders refuse the stream.
Channel mapping family 1 allows one to eight channels, but the header gives 9 (RFC 7845, section 5.1.1.2); decoders refuse the stream.
The identification header gives 2 coupled streams of 1, more coupled streams than streams (RFC 7845, section 5.1.1); decoders refuse the stream.
The identification header gives 0 streams, where at least one is required (RFC 7845, section 5.1.1); decoders refuse the stream.
1 entry of the channel mapping name a decoded channel the 2 the streams give do not include: the first, channel 1, names 7 (RFC 7845, section 5.1.1); decoders refuse the stream.
Channel mapping family 2 allows (1 + n)² + 2j channels for an ambisonic order n of 0 to 14 and j of 0 or 1 (1, 3, 4, 6, 9, 11, 16, 18, ...), but the header gives 5 (RFC 8486, section 3.3).

Channel mapping family 7 is reserved; decoders that do not know it should not decode the packets (RFC 8486, section 5.2, which updates RFC 7845, section 5.1.1.4). The analyzer reads its table in the format RFC 8486 recommends for new families.
The identification header holds 22 bytes, fewer than the 23 its channel mapping needs (RFC 7845, section 5.1.1); decoders refuse the stream.
The identification header holds 12 bytes, too few for its fields (RFC 7845, section 5.1); decoders refuse the stream, and its audio packets are read as single-stream packets.
The identification header holds 6 bytes after its fields, which decoders ignore.
